accepted.subject: fix: return a parsed PyJWKSet from the JWK Set cache (#1208)
accepted.brief:
In PyJWT, make the JWK Set cache used by `PyJWKClient` hold parsed key sets, and make key-set parsing tolerate malformed members.

1. `JWKSetCache.put(value)` accepts either an already parsed `PyJWKSet` or a raw JWKS payload (a dict), and always stores a parsed `PyJWKSet`, so `get()` returns a `PyJWKSet` (or None). Passing None still clears the cache. Any other value (for example a plain string) raises `PyJWKSetError` with the same message `PyJWKSet.from_dict` uses for an invalid set value.
2. `PyJWKClient.get_jwk_set()` returns a cached `PyJWKSet` as it is, without contacting the endpoint and without parsing again: repeated calls while the cache is valid return the very same object that `jwk_set_cache.get()` returns. A `PyJWKSet` that a caller put into the client's cache themselves must be accepted the same way (this used to fail with the error about the endpoint response not being a JSON object).
3. After a fresh fetch, `get_jwk_set()` caches the key set it actually returns. A subclass may override `fetch_data()` to filter or transform the payload; the next cache hit must serve the transformed key set, not the raw response (a key the subclass removed must not come back).
4. `fetch_data()` itself checks the endpoint response: when the endpoint does not return a JSON object, raise `PyJWKClientError` with the existing message about the endpoint response not being a JSON object (callers of `get_jwk_set()` see the same error as before).
5. `PyJWKSet.from_dict` skips members of the key list that are not JSON objects (None, strings, numbers) instead of crashing; if no workable key remains, it raises `PyJWKSetError` as for any set without workable keys. A member whose components have the wrong type (for example an RSA modulus given as a number) is an unworkable key: `PyJWK` must raise `InvalidKeyError` for it (a TypeError from the key loader is turned into `InvalidKeyError` like a ValueError), and a set containing only such keys raises `PyJWKSetError`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Throttle repeated PyJWKClient refreshes
accepted.brief:
In PyJWT, stop `PyJWKClient` from hammering the JWKS endpoint when tokens carry unknown key IDs.

1. `PyJWKClient(...)` takes a new keyword `cooldown_duration` (seconds, default 30). A negative value or a value that is not finite (NaN or infinity) raises `PyJWKClientError` at construction; the message starts with the words Cooldown duration (like the existing lifespan check names the lifespan).
2. Every successful fetch of the JWK Set (the first one, refreshes, fetches after the cache expired) records the time it happened, measured with `time.monotonic()` called through the `time` module imported in `jwt/jwks_client.py` (tests replace that function to control the clock).
3. `get_signing_key(kid)`: when the kid is not in the current set, it only forces a refresh from the endpoint if at least `cooldown_duration` seconds have passed since the last successful fetch; otherwise it raises the usual "unable to find a signing key" `PyJWKClientError` right away without contacting the endpoint. So two lookups of an unknown kid inside the cooldown cause a single request in total, while a lookup after the cooldown has passed refreshes again. A forced refresh also counts as a successful fetch.
4. The cooldown only applies when the JWK Set cache is enabled. With `cache_jwk_set=False` every lookup of an unknown kid still fetches and then refreshes once, as before. `cooldown_duration=0` disables the throttling.
5. `get_signing_key` is serialized with a lock held for the whole lookup (a re-entrant lock on the client), so concurrent lookups of an unknown kid do not each refresh: while one thread is refreshing, another thread missing the same kid waits for it and then, being inside the cooldown, fails without a second request.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working; a test that relied on an immediate refresh after a fetch now creates its client with no cooldown.

accepted.subject: Also take into account the count of subschema errors for relevance.
accepted.brief:
Improve `jsonschema.exceptions.best_match` for `anyOf` / `oneOf` errors whose subschemas fail at the same depth.

Today, when descending into the context errors of an `anyOf` or `oneOf` error, `best_match` groups the context errors by the subschema that produced them (the first element of each error's schema path), finds the most relevant error of each group, and stops (returning the `anyOf`/`oneOf` error itself) whenever the two best groups are equally relevant.

1. Rank each subschema group by the pair (relevance key of its most relevant error, number of errors in the group): among groups whose best errors are equally relevant, the group that produced fewer errors is better, because that subschema was closer to being valid. Descend into the error of the best-ranked group. Only when two or more groups have exactly the same rank (same key and same error count) stop descending and return the current error.
2. Consequences: for an instance where one subschema rejects every array item and another rejects only the single non-integer item, the best match is the `type` error about that non-integer item (whichever position it has), not the `anyOf`/`oneOf` error. For an object where one alternative fails on two properties and another fails only on a mismatched property type, the best match is that remaining `type` error, at that property's path.
3. Keep the existing tie-break inside a group: among equally relevant errors, the one appearing earlier in the instance wins, regardless of the order the context errors are listed in. Errors constructed by hand without any schema path all belong to one group (keyed by None), and the usual relevance key picks among them.
4. Compute each error's key only once.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working; the two existing tests that expected no traversal for such sibling errors now expect the traversal described in point 2.

accepted.subject: fix: restore support for falsy wait values and callable + strategy (#694)
accepted.brief:
Fix three runtime regressions in tenacity's wait handling that only show up once a retry actually happens.

1. Falsy `wait` values mean "no wait". Untyped callers construct `Retrying(wait=None)` or `Retrying(wait=0)`, and summing an empty list of wait strategies gives the int 0. Today such a retryer crashes with a `TypeError` from inside its iteration when it tries to call the wait value, which also hides the caller's real exception. When `wait` is falsy, the upcoming sleep must be 0 and the retry must go ahead normally, so a function that fails once and then succeeds returns its result. Do this for both the synchronous `Retrying` (`BaseRetrying._run_wait`) and `AsyncRetrying._run_wait` (for `None` and 0).
2. A plain callable plus a wait strategy. A plain function taking the retry state and returning a number is a valid wait (`WaitBaseT`), but functions have no `__add__`, so `func + wait_fixed(...)` goes through `wait_base.__radd__`, which today rejects it. Make `wait_base.__radd__` return a `wait_combine` of the strategy and the callable when the left operand is not a number; calling the result returns the sum of both waits. When the left operand is an int, keep treating 0 as the identity (return the strategy itself, so `sum()` over strategies works), and for any other number return `NotImplemented` so that, for example, adding a non-zero int to a strategy raises `TypeError` at the `+`.
3. `wait_combine` must accept plain callables among its strategies and call each one with the retry state passed positionally, not by the keyword `retry_state`, since a callable's parameter may have any name (a lambda with a differently named parameter must work). Its call returns the sum as a float.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: refactor: mark overridden methods with @override (#682)
accepted.brief:
In tenacity, mark every method that overrides a base-class method with an explicit override decorator (PEP 698), and provide that decorator from the package so tests and the library can share it.

1. Add `override` to `tenacity/_utils.py`, importable as `from tenacity._utils import override`. On Python 3.12 and later it is the standard library's `typing.override`. On older versions provide a backport with the same runtime behavior: it returns the decorated callable unchanged after setting its `__override__` attribute to True, silently skipping callables that do not allow attribute assignment. For type checkers (under `typing.TYPE_CHECKING`) import it from `typing_extensions`, which must never be imported at runtime.
2. Decorate with `@override` the methods in the library that override a base method: the `__repr__`/`__str__` of actions, `RetryError.__str__`, `BaseRetrying.__str__`/`__repr__`, `Retrying.__call__`, `RetryCallState.__repr__`, the overriding methods of `AsyncRetrying` (`__call__`, the `_run_*` hooks, `iter`, `__iter__`, `wraps`, ...), and the `__call__` (and operator) methods of the retry, stop and wait strategy classes, and the tornado retrying class. Do not decorate `BaseRetrying.__getstate__`, because `object.__getstate__` only exists from Python 3.11 on. The decorator must not change any behavior: decorated methods still work exactly as before, including methods on classes defined inside functions and dunder methods like `__pow__` on a float subclass.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: feat: add --local-version option to wheel pack (#694)
accepted.brief:
Add a `--local-version` option to the `wheel pack` command, to add, replace or remove the local version label (the part after `+`) of the wheel being repacked.

1. `wheel pack DIRECTORY [--dest DIR] [--build-number N] --local-version LABEL`; the option is passed through to `wheel._commands.pack.pack(directory, dest_dir, build_number, local_version=None)` as a new optional fourth parameter. Without the option nothing changes.
2. The new version is the existing version with any local label removed, followed by `+LABEL`; an empty LABEL removes the local label altogether. So a version without a label gains one, an existing label is replaced, and an empty argument strips it.
3. When a new version is computed, rename the unpacked `NAME-OLDVERSION.dist-info` directory to `NAME-NEWVERSION.dist-info`, and rewrite the `Version` field of its METADATA file to the new version (a missing METADATA file is a `WheelError`). The resulting wheel file name, the dist-info directory inside the archive and the METADATA version all use the new version; the rest of the wheel (for example the WHEEL file) is written as before.
4. Validate the new version with `packaging.version.Version`; if it is not a valid version, raise `WheelError` naming the invalid version. A label containing a hyphen must also be rejected with a `WheelError` whose message includes the label the user gave, because wheel file names cannot contain a hyphen in the version (tell the user to use an underscore instead). Through the command line (`wheel._commands.main()`), such errors make the command return exit code 1 and print the message (including the given label) to stderr.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Further improve soup contains performance
accepted.brief: Make soupsieve's `:-soup-contains(...)` fast when one pseudo-class lists many values. Today `CSSMatch.contains_text(el, text)` summarizes each element once per searched string (whether the element's text contains it, its length, and its first and last `len(text) - 1` characters, built from the children's summaries and cached in `CSSMatch.contains_cache` under the key `(id(element), text)`), and `match_contains` calls it once per value of the list. With a long list of values this repeats the whole summary work for every value. 1. Summarize each element once per value list instead: `contains_text(el, contain_list)` takes the `SelectorContains` object itself, and `contains_cache` is keyed by `(id(element), id(contain_list))`. An element's summary records whether its text contains any of the list's values, its length, and its first and last `n - 1` characters, where `n` is the length of the longest value. Search all values at once with one compiled regular expression of all of them (escaped, longest first), compiled once per list and kept in a new per-matcher dictionary that is cleared together with the other caches. A list that contains the empty string matches every element. 2. The number of entries in `contains_cache` for a document stays at most the number of elements checked, however many values a list has (a thousand values on a list of 32 items still gives at most 32 entries). After an element's parent has been summarized, the element's stored first/last characters are dropped (empty), exactly as today; only the topmost summarized element keeps them. 3. Results must be unchanged, for own-text matching too: an element matches when any value occurs in its text, including occurrences that cross the boundaries between text nodes and child elements (`abcd` contains `bcd`), with values of different lengths and repeated values in the same list, and with several `:-soup-contains` in one selector all required. Matches are the same with and without the `NOCACHE` flag. All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working; the existing test of which cache entries keep their ends now expects the new key form.

accepted.subject: Provide a fix for `:--soup-contains` performance and update perf notes
accepted.brief: Make soupsieve's `:-soup-contains(...)` take linear time on deeply nested documents. Today matching `:-soup-contains("text")` gets the full text of every candidate element and searches it; since an element's text includes all its descendants' text, a deeply nested document costs time quadratic in its depth. 1. Add `CSSMatch.contains_text(el, text)` and use it in `match_contains` for the non-own-text case whenever caching is enabled (with the `NOCACHE` flag keep today's way). It summarizes each element once per searched string, bottom-up from its children, and caches the summary in a new `CSSMatch.contains_cache` dictionary (cleared together with the other caches) under the key `(id(element), text)`. A summary is a tuple `(found, head, tail, length)`: whether the element's text contains `text`, the first and last `len(text) - 1` characters of its text, and its length. An occurrence that crosses the boundary between two children is found by searching the end of what precedes the boundary joined with the start of what follows it. Every text node is examined only once for a given string, so checking all the items of a document nested 32 levels deep examines at most 32 text nodes (count the calls to `CSSMatch.is_content_string`), for a pattern that matches nothing, one that matches everything, and one inside `:not()`. 2. The empty string is contained in every element. 3. Once an element's parent has been summarized, drop the element's first/last characters from its cache entry (store empty strings, keep `found` and `length`), so only the topmost summarized element keeps them; for a list of 32 nested items the cache then holds 32 entries and only the outermost one, keyed with the searched string, keeps its ends. 4. Text is taken as `get_text()` takes it: text across element boundaries joins up (`abc` contains `abc`, also through empty elements and across several levels), but comments and the contents of `template` elements are not part of the text, and whitespace between words matters (`a b c` does not contain `abc`). Several values in one `:-soup-contains(...)` still mean any of them. Results are identical with and without `NOCACHE`. All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Be consistent with how NOCACHE disables/enables caches
accepted.brief:
Make soupsieve's `NOCACHE` flag consistently disable every cache that depends on the document tree, and keep the one cache that does not depend on the tree always on.

Today `CSSMatch` keeps several per-call caches outside the `enable_cache` switch: the forms of a tree (used for `:default`, `:indeterminate`, radio groups), the selectedness of the options of a `select` (used for `option:checked`), the meta content-language of a document (used for `:lang()`), and the results of matching a language against a `:lang()`.

1. Under `NOCACHE`, the forms, option-selectedness and meta-language caches must be neither read nor written, so a lazy `iselect()` that modifies the tree while iterating sees the tree as it is when each element is matched. For example: when the content-language meta header is changed from one language to another after the first matching paragraph is yielded, the second paragraph no longer matches `p:lang(...)` of the first language; when a radio of a group gets checked after the first `:indeterminate` radio is yielded, the remaining radios of the group are no longer indeterminate; when another option of a `select` gets selected after the first `option:checked` is yielded, that option is reported as checked too. Rename these caches to `form_cache`, `option_cache` and `meta_lang_cache`, declare them with the other caches, and clear them in `reset()`.
2. The cache of language-match results (renamed `lang_match_cache`, keyed by the `:lang()` object and the language, not by any element) stays on even with `NOCACHE`, since nothing in it comes from the tree; it is cleared in `reset()` too. So for one select call, with or without `NOCACHE`, a long inherited language tag is validated at most once (one call of `RE_LANG_TAG.fullmatch`) and each language range is compared at most once (`CSSMatch.extended_language_filter` called at most once per range).
3. Document in `CSSMatch.__init__` the rule for caches: declared there, only used when `enable_cache` is true (except the language-match cache), cleared in `reset()`, keyed by element ids.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Fix `nth` selectors polynomial time cases
accepted.brief:
Fix polynomial running time of soupsieve's `nth` selectors (`:nth-child`, `:nth-last-child`, `:nth-of-type`, `:nth-last-of-type`, and their `of S` forms) when they are evaluated on siblings out of document order.

Today `CSSMatch.match_nth` caches, per parent and `nth` selector, only the last scanned position and index, and throws the cache away whenever an element is looked up before that position. Two situations look siblings up out of order: nested `of S` selectors where an outer `nth-last` selector walks the siblings in reverse while the inner one counts forward (or the other way round), and an `nth` selector inside `:has()` with a subsequent-sibling combinator (`p:has(~ :nth-child(...))`), whose search restarts at the next sibling of each element. Both re-scan the siblings again and again, so the work grows with the square (or higher powers, with more nesting) of the number of siblings.

1. Make the `nth` cache order-independent: per parent and `nth` selector (and, for `of-type`, per tag name and namespace), keep the 1-based position of every counted sibling found so far, keyed by the sibling's `id()`, plus how far the scan of the parent's contents has got and how many counted siblings were found; scanning only ever continues forward and never restarts. Positions for `last` selectors are derived from the total count once the whole parent has been scanned. Whether a sibling is counted (right tag type for `of-type`, matching `S` for `of S`) is evaluated at most once per sibling and selector.
2. Bound the work: with caching on, for a parent with n children, a selection makes at most 6n calls of the selector-matching method `CSSMatch._match_selectors`, for up to three levels of nested `of S` selectors in any combination of forward and last directions (also with `an+b` values other than `n` and with `of-type` at the innermost level), and for an `nth ... of S` selector inside `:has(~ ...)`, whether used directly, negated with `:not()`, or itself inside an outer `nth` selector's `of S`. The path without the cache may stay slow.
3. Results must stay correct, with and without `NOCACHE`, for nested `of S` selectors in any direction (including `an+b` forms like `-n+2`, `n+2`, `odd`, `2n`, fixed positions, and `of-type` inside `of S`), and for `nth` selectors inside `:has(~ ...)`, also inside `:not(...)` and inside another `nth` selector's `of S`. Elements without a parent element (top-level contents of a `template`) are still matched as before.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Fix more inconsistencies with :in-range and :out-of-range
accepted.brief:
Fix remaining inconsistencies in soupsieve's `:in-range` and `:out-of-range` pseudo-classes. Policy: follow the HTML spec, except where Chrome, Firefox and Safari all agree on something else.

1. Barred inputs: today only a `range` input is excluded from both pseudo-classes when it is barred from constraint validation. Apply the same exclusion to every input type these pseudo-classes handle (`number`, `date`, `month`, `week`, `time`, `datetime-local` as well as `range`): an input that is `disabled` (directly, or through a disabled `fieldset`, except inside that fieldset's first `legend`, which is not disabled), that has `readonly`, or that sits inside a `datalist` matches neither `:in-range` nor `:out-of-range`, whether its value is inside or outside its bounds. A non-barred input, including one in the first `legend` of a disabled `fieldset`, is evaluated as usual.
2. Upper limit on dates: browsers store date and time values as a JavaScript time, which ends at midnight UTC at the start of day 13 of month 9 of year 275760, and reject a value whose period starts after that moment. Treat such a value, `min` or `max` as invalid: for `date` the last valid day is that day 13; for `month` the last valid month is month 9 of that year; for `week` the last valid week is week 37 of that year; for `datetime-local` the last valid value is exactly that midnight (one millisecond later is invalid). The same applies to much larger years. An invalid value is sanitized to empty and is therefore in range; an invalid bound is ignored as if it were absent. So a valid value at the limit compared with an earlier `max` is out of range, while a value just past the limit is in range.
3. Strict bounds: a `min` or `max` must use the same strict syntax as a value, as browsers do (the spec's lenient parser for bounds is not followed). For `number` and `range`, a bound with leading or trailing whitespace, a leading `+`, trailing garbage letters, a trailing `.` with no digits after it, or an incomplete exponent is invalid and ignored. For `time` and `datetime-local`, a bound with more than three fractional second digits is invalid and ignored. A `range` input with an ignored bound falls back to its default (0 for the minimum, 100 for the maximum). Valid bounds keep working as before.
4. Implement the limit in `Inputs.parse_value` (it parses values, `min` and `max` alike) and the barring in the CSS patterns used for these pseudo-classes in `css_parser.py`; keep `CSSMatch.match_range` consistent, and document the policy and the known browser differences there.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Fix :in-range and :out-of-range for range inputs (#362)
accepted.brief:
Fix soupsieve's `:in-range` and `:out-of-range` for inputs whose type is `range`, following the HTML spec.

Today a `range` input is treated like a `number` input: it is only considered when it has a `min` or `max` attribute, and its value is compared against them, so a value below the minimum or above the maximum makes it out of range. That is wrong for `range`, whose value the browser clamps to its bounds.

1. A `range` input always has range limitations, even with no `min` or `max`: its minimum defaults to 0 and its maximum to 100. A `min` or `max` that does not parse is ignored and the default is used instead. The `type` attribute is matched case-insensitively, as for the other types.
2. Because its value is clamped, a `range` input is in range regardless of its value (missing, empty, invalid, below the minimum or above the maximum), as long as its effective maximum is not less than its effective minimum. If the effective maximum is less than the effective minimum (for example only a `min` above 100, only a negative `max`, an invalid `min` with a negative `max`, or an explicit `min` larger than `max`), it is out of range, whatever its value, including an empty one. So inputs that the existing number tests treat as out of range must all be in range when their type is `range`, and none of them out of range.
3. A `range` input that is barred from constraint validation matches neither pseudo-class: one that is disabled (directly or through a disabled `fieldset`, unless it is inside that fieldset's first `legend`), one with the `readonly` attribute, or one inside a `datalist`. An input inside the first `legend` of a disabled `fieldset` is not disabled and is evaluated as usual; one inside a later `legend` is disabled.
4. The other input types (`date`, `month`, `week`, `time`, `datetime-local`, `number`) keep their current behavior. Implement this in `CSSMatch.match_range` and in the `:in-range` / `:out-of-range` patterns in `css_parser.py`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Refactor method descriptor.
accepted.brief:
Refactor the `@cachedmethod` descriptor in cachetools and make class-level access return a stable object.

Today, every time a `@cachedmethod`-decorated method is looked up on the class rather than on an instance (for example `MyClass.method`), the descriptor's `__get__` builds a new wrapper and a new unbound function, so two lookups of the same method on the class give two different objects.

1. Class access identity: looking up a cached method on the class must return the same object every time, for every combination of decorator options (plain, with `info=True`, with a lock, with a condition, and their combinations). The unbound function is created once per descriptor, lazily, and shared by all class accesses, including lookups through a subclass that inherits the method without overriding it (the subclass and the base class get the same object). Different cached methods still return different objects. The unbound function keeps the wrapped method's metadata (via `functools.wraps`) and, when called with an instance as its first argument, behaves exactly like calling the method on that instance.
2. Do not build an instance wrapper on class access; build it only when the method is looked up on an instance (or, for the deprecated `@classmethod` use, when that path needs it).
3. Move the descriptor base classes and the two deprecation-warning helpers out of `src/cachetools/_cachedmethod.py` into a new private module `src/cachetools/_descriptor.py`: a method descriptor base (the current `_DescriptorBase`, renamed `_MethodDescriptor`) and a class-method descriptor base for the deprecated `@classmethod` support (the current `_DeprecatedDescriptorBase`, renamed `_ClassMethodDescriptor`), and have `_cachedmethod.py` import them. Instance behavior must not change: the per-instance wrapper is still stored in the instance `__dict__` (with the separate per-descriptor store for `super()` lookups), and the existing errors and deprecation warnings for instances without a usable `__dict__`, for assigning one descriptor to two names, and for use without `__set_name__` stay as they are.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: docstring_parser: give each problem a code
accepted.brief:
Give every problem reported by docstring_parser's `try_parse()` a stable code.

Today a `Problem` (in `docstring_parser/common.py`) is a named tuple of `line` and `message`, and the message is the only way to tell what went wrong. Messages may change between versions; add a short code that does not.

1. `Problem` gets a new field `code: str` between `line` and `message`, so its fields are, in order, `line`, `code`, `message`. Messages stay exactly as they are today.
2. The codes, and when each one is reported:
   - `bad-field`: a ReST or Epydoc field that cannot be read at all (for example a field whose head is not closed by a colon, or that has no name), and, in Epydoc, an unknown meta field whose key is shorter than two characters.
   - `wrong-arguments`: a field whose head has too many or too few words. In ReST: a param-kind field without one or two words after its key, or a returns, yields or raises field with more than one word after its key. In Epydoc: a param-kind field whose head does not have exactly one argument (including none at all), or a return field with any argument.
   - `mixed-returns-and-yields`: an Epydoc docstring that has both return and yield fields.
   - `missing-colon`: a Google item with no colon between its head and description, in a section that takes several items.
   - `missing-name`: a Google section of params that holds text and no named item.
   - `no-items`: a Google section whose items cannot be told apart by their indent.
3. Document every code in the docstring of `Problem`: each code on a line of its own, indented by exactly four spaces and written as the code in double backticks with nothing else on that line (reStructuredText definition-list style), followed by an indented explanation. Tools may read the set of valid codes from that docstring, so every code that can be reported must appear there in this form.
4. Add an `ItemError` subclass of `ParseError` in `common.py`, constructed as `ItemError(code, message)` and carrying the code in a `code` attribute; the Google and ReST item parsers raise it instead of a bare `ParseError`, and the code that collects problems turns it into a `Problem` with that code.
5. Robustness: for any docstring, including randomly corrupted ones (inserted punctuation, whitespace, section headers, field markers, deleted spans), in every style, `try_parse()` must report only problems whose code is documented in `Problem` and whose line is between 1 and the number of lines of the docstring as written; `parse()` must either raise a `ParseError` whose `problems` equal the problems from `try_parse()`, or, when `try_parse()` reports no problems, raise nothing. No other exception may escape.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: docstring_parser: give every style a Parser
accepted.brief:
Give every docstring style in docstring_parser a parser object.

Today only Google and Numpydoc have parser classes (`google.GoogleParser`, `numpydoc.NumpydocParser`); ReST and Epydoc parse with module-level functions, and auto-detection is a function in `docstring_parser/parser.py`. Make all of them objects with the same interface, built once with the sections they should recognise. Parsing output must not change at all.

1. Add a `BaseParser` class to `docstring_parser/common.py` and export it from the package (`from docstring_parser import BaseParser`). It has a class attribute `name`, the lower-case name of the style it reads, and a method `parse(text)` returning a `Docstring` (the base raises `NotImplementedError`).
2. Each style module gets a class named `Parser` deriving from `BaseParser`, constructed with an optional sequence of section specs (`None` means the style's default sections): `rest.Parser` (name `rest`), `google.Parser` (name `google`), `numpydoc.Parser` (name `numpydoc`), `epydoc.Parser` (name `epydoc`). The sections are read when the parser is built, not on every call. For every input, and both with no sections and with the style's default sections passed explicitly, `Parser(sections).parse(text)` must give exactly the same result as `parse(text, style, sections=sections)` (or raise a `ParseError` with the same message).
3. `google.GoogleParser` and `numpydoc.NumpydocParser` stay as aliases: the very same class objects as `google.Parser` and `numpydoc.Parser`. Their existing constructor options keep working.
4. Add a module `docstring_parser/auto.py` with a `Parser` (name `auto`) that holds one parser of every style, built with the sections it was given (each style receives the same sections), and parses a docstring in the style it is written in, exactly as auto-detection does today: it parses in every style and keeps the result with the most meta, preferring ReST, then Google, Numpydoc and Epydoc on a tie; if every style raises `ParseError`, it re-raises. `auto.Parser().parse(text)` must equal `parse(text)` for every input. The current shortcut (text in which no style can find a field or section is parsed as ReST only) must be turned off when any given section spec is `bare` (a title without a marker), so that, for example, a custom bare param section with an indented `name: description` item is detected as Google with that param.
5. The module-level `parse()` functions of each style and the top-level `parse(text, style, sections)` keep working, through a parser cached per list of sections in a module-level `ParserCache` named `_parsers` in each style module (for ReST, replace the current `_tables` cache), and one for auto-detection in `parser.py`. Calling `parse()` again with the same sections must reuse the cached parser, not build a new one: the list returned by `rest._parsers.parsers()` must not change.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: sections: find cached parsers by comparing lists
accepted.brief:
Speed up docstring_parser's lookup of parsers built for custom sections by adding a shared cache class.

Today `parse(text, style, sections=...)` looks up a parser for the given sections on every call. Google and Numpydoc key a plain dict on a tuple of the sections, so each call hashes every `SectionSpec` in Python; ReST and Epydoc rebuild their field table on every call. Passing a style's own default sections is therefore much slower than passing none.

1. Add a generic class `ParserCache` to `docstring_parser/sections.py`, constructed with an optional maximum size (default 16). Its `get(key, make, *args)` takes a list (of sections) as the key and returns the cached object whose stored list compares equal to it, or else calls `make(*args)`, stores the result as the most recent entry, drops the oldest entries beyond the size, and returns it. Keys are compared as lists, not hashed, so for the same section objects the comparison stops at identity. Its `parsers()` method returns the cached objects as a list, latest first.
2. Google: the module-level `google._parsers` becomes a `ParserCache` of `GoogleParser` objects, keyed on the list of the given sections or of `DEFAULT_SECTIONS` when none are given. Parsing again (including with no sections) must reuse the cached parser, so `google._parsers.parsers()` returns an equal list before and after a second `google.parse()` call.
3. Numpydoc: `numpydoc._parsers` becomes a `ParserCache` of `NumpydocParser` objects for explicitly given sections, keyed on a list of the sections followed by their titles (so that a title changed in place is not served a stale parser). The existing handling of the default parser stays.
4. ReST and Epydoc: cache the field tables built for given sections in a module-level `ParserCache` (named `_tables`) instead of rebuilding them on each call; for Epydoc, factor the table construction into a `_field_table(sections)` helper like ReST has.
5. Parsing output must not change.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: sections: declare sections alike in every style
accepted.brief:
Let docstring_parser users declare the sections (or fields) a style recognises in one way that works for every style.

Today each style has its own customisation: Google and Numpydoc have their own `Section` classes and decide what an item is by the section's key (a section must be keyed `param` to give params), while ReST and Epydoc have hard-coded field names. Add a style-independent declaration and accept it everywhere, without changing any output when it is not used.

1. New module `docstring_parser/sections.py` exporting `Kind` (the existing enum from `common`), `Layout`, `SectionSpec` and `default_sections`.
   - `Layout` is an enum with `ITEMS` (one item per entry), `BLOCK` (the whole body is one item) and `ITEM_OR_BLOCK` (items if the body starts like one, else one block, as Google's Returns reads).
   - `SectionSpec(titles, kind, key=None, layout=None, bare=False, parse_item=None)`. `titles` is one string or an iterable of strings, stored as a tuple; an empty one raises `ValueError` saying a section needs at least one title. `key` defaults to the kind's usual key (`param`, `keyword`, `other_param`, `receives`, `attribute`, `returns`, `yields`, `raises`, `warns`, `examples`, `deprecation`), and for a text section to its first title in lower case with spaces replaced by underscores (so a text section titled with two words separated by a space gets the key with an underscore). `layout` defaults to `BLOCK` for text, examples and deprecation, `ITEM_OR_BLOCK` for returns and yields, and `ITEMS` otherwise. Specs compare equal when all their attributes are equal, and are hashable.
   - `default_sections(style)` returns the list of specs a style uses when given none (each style module gets a `default_sections()` function). For auto mode it raises `ValueError` saying the style has none of its own.
2. Accept a list of specs as `sections` in the top-level `parse()` and `parse_from_object()`, in each style module's `parse()`, and in `GoogleParser` and `NumpydocParser` (which keep accepting their old `Section` objects too). Given sections replace the style's own: a section or field not in the list is not recognised (a Google section left out stays in the long description as text; a ReST field left out becomes plain meta keyed by its name, not a raises entry). Passing a style's default sections explicitly must give exactly the same output (or the same `ParseError` message) as passing none, for every case file. In auto mode, the sections go to every style.
3. A spec's kind decides the kind and class of its items, whatever its key. In Google and Numpydoc, titles are section titles; in ReST and Epydoc, they are field names, and each item's `key` is the name the field was written with. Examples: a Google section with two titles and kind `OTHER_PARAM` gives params with key `other_param` and their names and types; a Numpydoc section with kind `KEYWORD` and its own key gives params with that key, name, type and description; a ReST field declared with two names and kind `PARAM`, written with a type and a name, gives a `DocstringParam` keyed by the written name with that name and type, and a ReST field of kind `WARNS` gives an entry in `raises` with its type; an Epydoc field of kind `PARAM` combines with an Epydoc type field for the same name, and an Epydoc field of kind `DEPRECATION` sets `docstring.deprecation` with its own key.
4. `bare=True` means the title stands alone on its line: in Google with no colon after it, in Numpydoc with no underline below it (the title is matched exactly, even if it contains markup characters such as asterisks). Bare and normal sections can be mixed in one docstring.
5. `parse_item`, if given, is called with each item's meta after it has been split into name, type and description; if it returns `None`, the (possibly modified) meta is kept; if it returns a meta, that meta is used as it is instead.
6. Composing: a docstring with items of any kind from a section with an unusual key must compose in every style and rendering style without raising or dropping the item; the item's description must appear in the output.
7. The Google module caches parsers in a module-level dict `_parsers`, keyed by a tuple of the sections (or of `DEFAULT_SECTIONS` when none are given), holding at most 16 parsers. A second `google.parse()` call with the same (default) sections must reuse the cached parser, so the dict's values do not change.
8. Existing ways of customising parsing by subclassing or overriding keep working.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: google+numpydoc: keep every param in compose
accepted.brief:
Make docstring_parser's Google and Numpydoc `compose()` keep every param instead of silently dropping some.

Today Google's `compose()` writes into its `Args:` section only params whose first arg (`args[0]`) is exactly `param`, and Numpydoc's writes into `Parameters` only those keyed `param`. So params parsed from ReST fields such as `:keyword:`, `:arg:`, `:argument:`, `:key:` or `:parameter:` disappear when the docstring is composed as Google or Numpydoc, and Numpydoc's other params and received params disappear when composed as Google. ReST's `:ivar:`, `:var:` and `:cvar:` fields parse as plain `DocstringMeta` (not params), and are composed as a nameless section of their own.

1. Google `compose()`: the `Args:` section gets every param except attributes (keyword, other, received and other aliased params included), in the order they appear. Numpydoc `compose()`: the `Parameters` section gets every param except attributes, other params and received params (which have sections of their own in Numpydoc).
2. Add to `docstring_parser/common.py` a set `ATTRIBUTE_FIELD_KEYWORDS` of the ReST attribute field names (`ivar`, `var`, `cvar`) and a function `meta_as_attribute(meta)` that, for a plain `DocstringMeta` (exactly that class, not a subclass) whose `args` are two items with the first one an attribute field name, returns a `DocstringParam` with `args` of the attribute key and the name, the same description, that name as `arg_name` and no type, optionality or default; for anything else it returns `None`.
3. In both Google and Numpydoc `compose()`, such attribute fields are written as named items in the attributes section (after the real attribute params) and are no longer written as a separate untitled section.
4. Round trip: parsing a ReST docstring with a `:param:`, a `:keyword:`, an `:arg:`, a `:parameter:` and an `:ivar:` field, composing it as Google or as Numpydoc and parsing the result in that style must give five params in that order: the first four as params (key `param`) with their names and descriptions, and the last as an attribute with its name and description. Parsing a Numpydoc docstring with an "Other Parameters" entry that has a type and a "Receives" entry without one, composing it as Google and parsing it back as Google must give both params, in order, with the first's type kept and no type for the second.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: common: normalise line endings before parsing
accepted.brief:
Make docstring_parser handle Windows (`
`) and old Mac (``) line endings in every style.

`inspect.cleandoc` splits lines on `
` only, so today docstrings with `
` or `` endings keep a stray `` in their descriptions; and from Python 3.13 on, cleandoc measures indentation by stripping spaces only, so a blank line holding just `` counts as unindented text, nothing is dedented, and fields are not found at all.

1. Add `normalize_line_endings(text)` to `docstring_parser/common.py`, which turns every `
` and every lone `` into `
`.
2. Every style parser (ReST, Google, Numpydoc, Epydoc) must normalise line endings before it cleans or otherwise processes the text, so that a docstring written with `
` or with `` endings parses exactly like the same docstring with `
` endings: same short description, same long description, same meta items with the same `args` and the same descriptions (no `` left anywhere). This must hold for an indented docstring with a summary, a long description, a param and a returns entry in each style, on every supported Python version.
3. Consequently, text that ReST keeps outside its fields (for example a trailing example block after the field list) uses `
` line endings in the result even when the input used `
`; the ReST field-splitting pattern can then match plain `
` instead of optional `
`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Validate response_mode before returning redirectable authorization errors
accepted.brief:
Validate `response_mode` in oauthlib's OAuth 2 authorization flows before any error is redirected to the client.

Today `GrantTypeBase.prepare_authorization_response` silently replaces an unsupported `response_mode` with the grant's default, and the mode is only defaulted there, so errors raised during validation do not know which mode to use (implicit and hybrid errors end up in the query instead of the fragment), and a duplicated `response_mode` parameter is accepted.

1. New error `UnsupportedResponseModeError`, a subclass of `InvalidRequestFatalError` in `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/errors.py`, exported from `oauthlib.oauth2`, with a description saying the `response_mode` parameter is unsupported. Being fatal, it is never redirected: it surfaces as an exception with status code 400.
2. Add `GrantTypeBase._validate_response_mode(request)`: a response mode is supported if it is `query` or `fragment`, or equals the grant's own `default_response_mode` (a subclass may set another default, such as `form_post`, which is then accepted). If `request.response_mode` is set (non-empty) and unsupported, raise `UnsupportedResponseModeError`; otherwise set it to the given mode or, when missing or empty, to the grant's default. `prepare_authorization_response` uses it instead of the silent fallback, so calling it directly with an unsupported mode raises.
3. `ImplicitGrant` declares `default_response_mode = 'fragment'` explicitly.
4. In `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_authorization_request` and `ImplicitGrant.validate_token_request` (which backs the implicit grant's `validate_authorization_request`): treat a repeated `response_mode` parameter like the other duplicated parameters (a fatal invalid-request error naming the duplicated parameter), and validate and default the response mode right after the redirect URI checks, before any normal error is raised and before the response type is validated (the validator's `validate_response_type` must not be called for an unsupported mode). This applies to the OpenID Connect hybrid grant too, whatever its response type (valid, invalid or missing).
5. Custom validators may change the response mode, so validate it again when request validation finishes (a decorator `revalidate_response_mode` in `grant_types/base.py` applied to those two methods works), whether the validation returned or raised a normal `OAuth2Error`: an unsupported mode then takes precedence and `UnsupportedResponseModeError` is raised instead of the normal error, without being chained to it (its `__context__` is `None`). A fatal client error passes through unchanged. When the normal error is re-raised, its `response_mode` is set to the request's (defaulted) mode, even if the error was created without a request.
6. As a result, a normal error raised during validation carries the response mode, and its `in_uri()` uses the fragment when that mode is `fragment`: so implicit and hybrid errors (for example an unauthorized client or an invalid scope) go in the fragment by default, while authorization code errors use the grant's default mode or the requested one.
7. In `AuthorizationCodeGrant.create_authorization_response` and `ImplicitGrant.create_token_response`, when validation raises a normal error, validate the response mode before redirecting (an unsupported mode, including one set by a pre-auth or post-auth custom validator that raised or not, raises `UnsupportedResponseModeError` instead of redirecting). The authorization code grant puts error parameters in the fragment only for mode `fragment` and in the query otherwise; the implicit grant puts them in the fragment unless the mode is `query` (so a subclass whose default is `form_post` still returns errors in the fragment). On success, after the code modifiers or token modifiers have run, validate the response mode again before anything is saved: an unsupported mode set by a modifier or a post-auth validator raises, and neither `save_token` nor `save_authorization_code` is called.
8. A subclass whose default mode is `form_post` can handle it in its own `prepare_authorization_response`: with no mode or `form_post` requested it is used, `query` still redirects with the code in the query, and any other mode (for example `web_message`) raises `UnsupportedResponseModeError`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Organized validate_client functions for all grant to avoid mistake in grnat implementation
accepted.brief:
Centralise client authentication in oauthlib's OAuth 2 token grants so every grant checks the authenticated client the same way.

Today each grant type (authorization code, client credentials, refresh token, resource owner password credentials, device code) repeats its own variant of authenticating the client, checking that `request.client` has a `client_id`, and filling `request.client_id` from it; the variants differ (some skip the check, one checks only for public clients, none notices a mismatch).

1. Add to `GrantTypeBase` (in `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/base.py`):
   - `validate_client_confidential(request)`: call the validator's `authenticate_client(request)`; if it fails, raise `InvalidClientError`.
   - `validate_client_public(request)`: call the validator's `authenticate_client_id(request.client_id, request)`; if it fails, raise `InvalidClientError`.
   - In both, after successful authentication: if `request.client` is `None` or has no `client_id` attribute, raise `NotImplementedError` explaining that the validator must set `request.client` with a `client_id`; if `request.client_id` is empty, set it from `request.client.client_id`; if it is set but differs from `request.client.client_id`, raise `errors.ServerError` (a discrepancy between client identifiers).
   - `validate_client_authentication(request)` calls `validate_client_confidential` when the validator's `client_authentication_required(request)` is true and `validate_client_public` otherwise.
2. Use these everywhere instead of the per-grant code: the authorization code, refresh token and device code grants call `validate_client_authentication` and drop their own `client_id` checks and assignments; the client credentials grant calls `validate_client_confidential` (so a failed authentication there still gives an `invalid_client` error response); the resource owner password credentials grant moves its client authentication from `create_token_response` into `validate_token_request`, right after checking the grant type, and drops its own `client_id` handling after `validate_user`.
3. Examples that must hold for `validate_token_request`: in the authorization code grant and the refresh token grant, a confidential client whose `authenticate_client` sets `request.client` with a different `client_id` than the request's raises `ServerError`; in the authorization code grant, a public client whose `authenticate_client_id` succeeds but leaves a `request.client` without `client_id` raises `NotImplementedError`, and one that sets a client with a different `client_id` raises `ServerError`. Validators that set `request.client.client_id` equal to the request's `client_id` keep working in every grant, including the device code grant's token response and custom pre/post token validators.
4. Update the docstrings of `RequestValidator.authenticate_client_id` and `validate_client_id` to say they must set `request.client` to a client object with a non-empty `client_id`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: BUG: Fix node connectivity and node cuts for digraphs (#8837)
accepted.brief:
Fix networkx's `node_connectivity` and `minimum_node_cut` (in `networkx/algorithms/connectivity/`) for directed graphs, and make both ignore self-loops and parallel edges.

Both functions implement algorithm 11 of Esfahanian's "Connectivity Algorithms", which is stated for undirected graphs; the current adaptation to digraphs returns values that are too large, and `minimum_node_cut` can return a set that is not a cut at all. Fix these defects, for every flow function:

1. Starting node and bound. The node with minimum degree is chosen with `G.degree`, which counts parallel edges and self-loops and, for a digraph, the total of in- and out-degree. Instead, use the number of distinct neighbors other than the node itself: for an undirected graph, its distinct neighbors; for a digraph, the smaller of its number of distinct predecessors and its number of distinct successors (isolating a node only requires removing all its predecessors or all its successors). This value is the initial bound in `node_connectivity`. So a complete graph on five nodes with a self-loop on every node, or a complete multigraph on five nodes with every edge doubled, has node connectivity 4, both as given and converted to a digraph; and a weakly connected digraph that is not strongly connected, in which some node has no predecessors, has node connectivity 0.
2. Initial cutset. `minimum_node_cut` starts from the successors of the starting node only, which does not isolate a node that also has predecessors and is empty for a node with no successors. Start instead from the set that isolates the chosen node: for a digraph the smaller of its distinct predecessors and its distinct successors, for an undirected graph its distinct neighbors, never including the node itself. So the minimum node cut of a complete graph on five nodes with self-loops (and of its directed version) has 4 nodes, and the minimum node cut of the directed 3-cycle has one node, whose removal leaves the digraph not strongly connected, and has the same size as its node connectivity.
3. Neighbor pairs. For a digraph, the neighbors of the starting node are built by chaining its predecessors and successors, so a node that is both appears twice and is paired with itself. Use the set of distinct neighbors, without the node itself, both to choose the non-neighbors and to form the pairs of neighbors.
4. Reverse edges. `minimum_st_node_cut(G, s, t)` returns the empty set when there is an edge in either direction between `s` and `t`. Only an edge from `s` to `t` makes the pair inseparable; in a digraph an edge from `t` to `s` is not an `s`-`t` path. So in the directed 3-cycle 0->1->2->0, the minimum node cut from 0 to 2 is the middle node 1, and from 0 to 1 it is empty. For undirected graphs nothing changes.
5. Both orders. The local node connectivity of an ordered pair in a digraph is not symmetric, and the starting node must be tried both as source and as target against each of its non-neighbors (Even and Tarjan, 1975). In `node_connectivity`, take the minimum of `local_node_connectivity` over both orders; in `minimum_node_cut`, compute the `s`-`t` node cut for both orders and keep the smallest. For example, a weakly connected digraph in which some node cannot reach the starting node has node connectivity 0 and an empty minimum node cut, even when the local connectivity in the other direction is 1; and a strongly connected digraph whose single node removal disconnects it has node connectivity 1 and a minimum node cut of size 1 (not 2), whose removal leaves it not strongly connected.

Also update the docstrings to describe this behavior for digraphs.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: MAINT: allow isomorphism match helpers to be lists or not (#8803)
accepted.brief:
Let networkx's isomorphism match helpers (`networkx/algorithms/isomorphism/matchhelpers.py`) accept a single `default` (and `op`) for a list of attributes, and reject lists of the wrong length.

Today, when `attr` is a list, `categorical_node_match`, `categorical_multiedge_match`, `numerical_node_match`, `numerical_multiedge_match`, `generic_node_match` and `generic_multiedge_match` zip `attr` with `default` (and `op`) as lists: a single non-list `default` or `op` fails, and lists of a different length than `attr` are silently truncated.

1. When `attr` is a list and `default` is not a list, use that one default value for every attribute. When `default` is a list, it must have the same length as `attr`. The same applies to `op` in `generic_node_match` and `generic_multiedge_match`: a single callable is used for every attribute, a list must have the same length as `attr`. Any combination of list and non-list `default` and `op` is allowed. When `attr` is a single string, behavior is unchanged (and a list `default` or `op` given with a string `attr` is accepted when the helper is built).
2. A length mismatch between `attr` and a list `default` or list `op` must raise `ValueError` when the helper is built (not when it is called), with a message that starts like the one Python's built-in `zip(..., strict=True)` produces for unequal lengths. Using `zip(..., strict=True)` gives exactly that; where you check lengths by hand (as for `op` in `generic_multiedge_match`), word the message the same way.
3. Fix `generic_multiedge_match` with several attributes: each attribute must be compared with its own operator (the operators are applied per attribute, in order, to the values of the two edges), trying every pairing of the parallel edges; it returns true if some pairing matches all attributes of all edges, else false. So helpers combining different operators for different attributes (for example equality for an id and an element-wise comparison for a tuple-valued attribute), a single operator for several attributes, and lists of defaults and operators all match two multiedge sets with the same attribute values in a different order, and do not match when the edge ids differ. Missing attributes take their default.
4. Update the docstrings to describe the accepted forms of `default` and `op`.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: BUG: Fix k_components losing or truncating k-components (#8734)
accepted.brief:
Fix networkx's exact `k_components` (`networkx/algorithms/connectivity/kcomponents.py`), which can lose or truncate k-components.

Two helpers are wrong:

1. `_generate_partition(G, cuts, k)` removes the union of all minimum cutsets in a single pass and then re-attaches cutset nodes that have a neighbor in a remaining component. A cutset node whose neighbors all lie in other cutsets is dropped, so a k-component can be lost. Apply the cutsets one at a time instead, as in Moody and White (2003), appendix A, step 3: starting from the set of all nodes, find a cutset that is a proper subset of the current set of nodes and whose removal splits it into two or more connected components; each component, plus the nodes of that cutset that have at least one neighbor in the component, becomes a new candidate part (avoid processing the same part twice), and is split further in the same way. A part that no cutset splits any further is kept if it is smaller than the whole graph. Then merge parts that share at least k+1 nodes (the existing `_consolidate(parts, k + 1)`) as a performance step; if merging would rebuild a part as large as the whole graph, yield the unmerged parts instead, so the caller always recurses on strictly smaller graphs. Every j-component with j > k must end up intact in at least one part.
2. `_reconstruct_k_components` skips propagating a component from level k+1 down to level k whenever the union of the components already recorded at level k covers its nodes, so fragments can replace a genuine k-component. Propagate a level-(k+1) component down unless it is a subset of a single component recorded at level k.

Examples that must hold: take two icosahedral graphs (5-connected, on nodes 0-11 and 12-23), add three connector nodes each joined to three nodes of the first and two of the second icosahedron, and a fourth node joined to two nodes of each, so the whole graph is 4-connected. Then `k_components` must report exactly the two icosahedra as its 5-components, and the whole graph as the single k-component for every k from 1 to 4. A random graph on 16 nodes whose node connectivity is 7 must have the whole node set as its single k-component for every k from 1 to 7. The approximation algorithm `networkx.algorithms.approximation.k_components` must give the same results on these two graphs.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Report template location for compile time warnings
accepted.brief:
Report Python compile-time warnings in Mako templates (in practice `SyntaxWarning`, such as an invalid escape sequence in a string inside a `<% %>` block) at their location in the template.

Today such a warning is reported against the generated Python module, with a line number unrelated to the template, and it is reported twice: once while the individual expression is parsed (filename `<unknown>`, line 1) and again when the whole module is compiled.

1. In `mako/pyparser.py`, name the filename used when parsing individual expressions in a module constant `EXPRESSION_FILENAME` (its value stays `<unknown>`).
2. In `mako/template.py`, while a template is compiled, replace the warnings display hook (`warnings.showwarning`) temporarily, restoring it afterwards, instead of recording and re-raising warnings, so each warning passes through the warnings filters exactly once:
   - While the template source is generated (expressions parsed), drop warnings whose filename is `EXPRESSION_FILENAME`. Because the same warning is passed over by the filters first at this point, a filter with action `once` would record it and suppress the later, useful occurrence; remove that record from `warnings.onceregistry` when dropping it. Warnings with other filenames are shown unchanged.
   - While the generated module is compiled and its module-level code (the `<%! %>` blocks) is executed, show a warning whose filename is the generated module's id (for a template compiled in memory) or the generated module file's path (for a template compiled to a `module_directory`, where the import system compiles it) against the template's filename (for a template from a string, its `uri`), with the line number translated through the module's full line map, the same one used to locate exceptions in templates. The module source is read only when needed. If the line cannot be translated, or the module's metadata cannot be read (for example a source without Mako metadata), show the warning unchanged rather than failing. Warnings with any other filename, such as one raised by a module imported from a `<%! %>` block (even one that uses the filename `<unknown>`), are shown unchanged. Provide this as a context manager `_translate_module_warnings(get_source, module_id, filename)` in `mako/template.py`, where `get_source` is a callable returning the generated module source.
   - This must apply the same way to templates compiled from a string, from a file, and from a file with a module directory.
3. Resulting behavior: a warning in a code block on line 4 of the template is reported once, with the template's filename and line 4, regardless of how many lines precede the block; warnings in a `<%! %>` block and in a `${}` expression are each reported once at their template lines; a `warnings.warn` call executed in a `<%! %>` block is reported at its template line; this holds for the filter actions `always`, `default`, `module` and `once`. With the filter action `error`, compilation raises a `SyntaxException` carrying the warning's message (from parsing the expression), as today. A template without problems raises no warnings.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Treat empty string comments as no comment in autogenerate
accepted.brief:
Treat an empty-string table or column comment like no comment in Alembic's autogenerate comparison, and stop dropping empty-string comments when rendering and emitting DDL.

PostgreSQL (setting a comment to the empty string removes it), MySQL/MariaDB and Oracle do not store an empty comment distinctly from no comment, so it reflects back as `None`; today autogenerate then detects a comment change on every run. At the same time, several places test `if comment:`, so an explicit empty-string comment is never rendered or emitted.

1. Comparison (`alembic/autogenerate/compare/comments.py`): normalise comments with a helper that turns an empty string into `None`, and use the normalised values in both the column and the table comment comparators. So any combination of empty string and `None` on the database and metadata sides produces no diff for columns or tables. A column whose comment goes from empty to non-empty, or from non-empty to empty, produces a `modify_comment` diff whose existing and new comment values are the normalised ones (`None` for the empty side). A table whose comment goes from empty to non-empty produces an `add_table_comment` diff with the new comment on the table and `None` as the existing comment; one whose comment goes from non-empty to empty produces a `remove_table_comment` diff whose table has no comment.
2. Rendering (`alembic/autogenerate/render.py`): render a `comment=` argument whenever the comment is not `None`, including the empty string, both for columns (`_render_column`, so also inside `op.add_column` and `op.create_table`) and for the table in `op.create_table`.
3. DDL: `DefaultImpl.create_table` (comments emitted separately on dialects without inline comments), `toimpl.add_column`, and the MySQL column specification must emit a comment whenever it is not `None`. So on PostgreSQL, adding a column with an empty comment emits the `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` followed by a `COMMENT ON COLUMN ... IS ''` statement, and creating a table with an empty table comment and an empty comment on one column emits the `CREATE TABLE` followed by `COMMENT ON TABLE` and then `COMMENT ON COLUMN` statements with empty strings; on MySQL, adding a column with an empty comment emits an inline `COMMENT ''` in the column specification.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Strip PostgreSQL type cast specifiers when comparing computed defaults
accepted.brief:
Strip PostgreSQL type casts before Alembic's autogenerate compares computed column expressions and expression-based indexes.

PostgreSQL stores computed-column expressions and index expressions with `::type` casts added (for example a string literal cast to `regconfig` or `"char"`, a column cast to `text`, a number cast to `numeric(10,2)` or `double precision`, a literal cast to `timestamp(3) without time zone`, an array cast to `text[]`, a literal cast to a schema-qualified quoted enum type). Today the reflected expression then differs from the metadata expression, so autogenerate emits a false "Computed default on <table>.<column> cannot be modified" warning for unchanged computed columns, and reports unchanged expression indexes whose expression contains certain casts as modified.

1. Move the computed-default normalisation from a module function in `alembic/autogenerate/compare/server_defaults.py` to a method `_normalize_computed_default(sqltext)` on `DefaultImpl` (same behavior as today: drop spaces, parentheses, quotes, backticks, brackets, tabs and newlines, and lower-case), and have the comparator call it on the migration context's impl for both the metadata and the reflected expression.
2. `PostgresqlImpl._normalize_computed_default` first removes every `::` cast with a complete type name from the text, then applies the default normalisation. A complete type name is a plain or double-quoted identifier, optionally schema-qualified (also quoted), optionally followed by `varying` or `precision`, an optional length or precision/scale in parentheses (one or two integers), an optional `with time zone` / `without time zone`, and any number of array brackets; matching is case-insensitive, and SQL following the type name is left intact. So the reflected forms of expressions such as a weighted text-search vector, a lower-cased column compared to NULL, two equality tests joined with AND, a CASE expression, arithmetic with casts to numeric or double precision, a comparison with a timestamp literal, an ANY over an array, and a comparison with an enum literal normalise to the same text as the plain metadata expressions.
3. As a result, on PostgreSQL, comparing a table with an unchanged computed column produces no diff and no warning for such expressions, while a computed column whose expression really changed (a different literal, function, operator or column) still produces no diff but emits exactly one warning that the computed default on that table and column cannot be modified.
4. Expression indexes (`PostgresqlImpl._cleanup_index_expr`): strip `::` casts with the same complete-type-name pattern (instead of the current loose pattern), and strip `CAST(expr AS type)` with a complete type name, repeating until no cast is left so nested casts are removed. A column whose name ends in the letters of the `AS` keyword must not be mistaken for it. So unchanged indexes on a column cast to `Text`, on a column cast to `Numeric(10, 2)`, on a column cast to `String(10)`, and on a nested cast to `Numeric(10, 2)` then `Text` are not reported as changed.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Establish a single producer for type-bound CHECK constraints in batch
accepted.brief:
Fix how Alembic's batch "recreate" mode (`alembic/operations/batch.py`) names CHECK constraints, for constraints generated by a `SchemaType` (such as `Boolean` or `Enum` with `create_constraint=True`) and for reflected constraints, when a naming convention is involved.

Today batch recreate has two independent producers of a type-bound CHECK constraint when a column is added: the explicit `add_constraint()` queued by the `add_column` operation, and the column type's own attach-time event firing against the temporary `_alembic_tmp_` table, which knows neither the naming convention nor the real table name, so the constraint can be duplicated or misnamed. Also, when `naming_convention` is passed to `batch_alter_table`, it is applied to the reflected table's metadata, so names that came back from reflection (already the real names in the database) are elaborated a second time.

1. `ApplyBatchImpl.add_column()`: after copying the column, turn off the schema events of its type when it is a `SchemaEventTarget` (set both its `_create_events` and its `create_constraint` to false), so the queued `add_constraint()` is the only producer of its CHECK constraint, as it already is for `alter_column()`. So adding, in batch mode with a convention whose `ck` template is `ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s`, a non-nullable `Boolean` or `Enum` column whose type has its own name gives exactly one CHECK constraint, named by the convention from the real table name and the type's name; without a convention, the constraint takes the type's own name.
2. When building the new table, name the type-bound constraints that a type regenerates onto it (as happens for columns carried over from a `Table` passed as `copy_from`) using the naming convention of the metadata of the table being replaced, resolved against that table so `%(table_name)s` gives the real name, not the temporary one. Put this in a helper `_name_type_bound_constraints(table, source_table)` in `alembic/util/sqla_compat.py`; it does nothing when the source metadata has no naming convention. So recreating a table that has a convention-named `Boolean` CHECK constraint, with `copy_from` and `recreate="always"`, keeps exactly that constraint name.
3. If the convention needs `%(constraint_name)s` but the type has no name of its own, leave the constraint unnamed and emit an Alembic warning (via `alembic.util.warn`) whose message is: "The CHECK constraint generated by the type of column '<table>.<columns>' has no name, while the naming convention in use requires one; the constraint is emitted without a name." followed by a hint that `Boolean` and `Enum` datatypes should be given a name (e.g. `Boolean(name='...')`) for their CHECK constraints to participate fully in batch mode. The recreated table then has the constraint without a name.
4. When the table is reflected and `naming_convention` was given: reflect into a plain `MetaData`, mark every reflected constraint and index name that is a string as final with `sqlalchemy.schema.conv` (helper `_conv_constraint_names(table)` in `sqla_compat.py`), and then copy the table into a `MetaData` that has the naming convention, so the convention only names constraints reflected without a name. So a reflected CHECK constraint that already has a convention-style name keeps exactly that name after a batch recreate with the same convention, and an unnamed reflected CHECK constraint gets the name the convention gives it (for example with a `ck` template made of the table name and a fixed suffix).

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Make named CHECK constraint autogenerate opt-in
accepted.brief:
Make Alembic's autogenerate plugin that detects named CHECK constraints opt-in, rename it, and keep the old name working.

The plugin was added recently and is enabled by default through the default `autogenerate_plugins` wildcard `alembic.autogenerate.*`. Its comparison is by name only, so a CHECK constraint that is unnamed on the metadata side cannot be matched with the one reflected from the database (PostgreSQL names every constraint), which produces false removals for users who never asked for CHECK constraint detection, including for type-bound constraints of `Enum`/`Boolean` with `create_constraint=True`.

1. Move the plugin module from `alembic/autogenerate/compare/check_constraints.py` to a new package `alembic/ext/` as `alembic/ext/checkconstraint_byname.py` (with an `alembic/ext/__init__.py`), and register it under the plugin name `alembic.ext.checkconstraint_byname`, so the default wildcard no longer matches it. It takes effect only when named explicitly in `EnvironmentContext.configure(autogenerate_plugins=[...])`. With the defaults, adding or removing a named CHECK constraint produces no diff, and reflected CHECK constraints are no longer passed to `include_name` (the default comparison no longer looks at them). Update the `autogenerate_plugins` documentation accordingly.
2. Legacy name: in `alembic/runtime/plugins.py`, add `_translate_legacy_name(name)` that maps the former full name `alembic.autogenerate.checkconstraint_byname` to `alembic.ext.checkconstraint_byname` and returns any other name unchanged (current names, unknown names and wildcard expressions such as `alembic.autogenerate.*` are never translated). `Plugin.populate_autogenerate_priority_dispatch` applies it to every included name and to every `~` exclusion, so the old name both enables the plugin and, after `~`, excludes it (for example together with `alembic.ext.*`, the exclusion still removes only this plugin). The error raised for included names that match no plugin must still report each name as the user wrote it, not its translation.
3. With the plugin enabled (by either name), behavior for regular named and unnamed CHECK constraints, schemas, `include_name`/`include_object` filters, backends without CHECK reflection, and naming conventions stays as before. Type-bound constraints now take part in the comparison: `sqla_compat.all_table_check_constraints(table)` returns all CHECK constraints of the table and its columns, including type-bound ones. So adding a column whose non-native `Enum` (with `create_constraint=True`) has a name reports an `add_constraint` for a constraint with that name, while one whose type has no name reports no CHECK constraint change; changing such a named type to a type without a constraint (or to the same type with `create_constraint=False`) reports a `remove_constraint` with that name; for an unnamed one, a removal is reported only on backends that name unnamed constraints, and then with the reflected name. Identical tables with a named type-bound `Enum` or `Boolean` constraint produce no diff whether the plugin is enabled or not.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Fix callback exception handling to be per-Connection instead of per-Context (#1535)
accepted.brief:
Keep exceptions raised in pyOpenSSL callbacks with the `Connection` whose callback raised them, instead of on the callback wrapper shared by every connection of a `Context` (`src/OpenSSL/SSL.py`).

Exceptions raised inside the verify, ALPN selection, OCSP (server and client) and DTLS cookie generate/verify callbacks cannot be raised from inside the callback, so today they are stored in a list on the callback helper object (`_CallbackExceptionHelper._problems`) and re-raised by `Connection._raise_ssl_error` (or `DTLSv1_listen`) on the next operation. For callbacks registered on a `Context`, that helper is shared by every connection made from the context, so with connections driven from several threads one connection can be handed another connection's exception. Also, `_raise_ssl_error` only consults the context's helpers, so an exception from a verify callback set with `Connection.set_verify` (which uses a helper of its own) is never raised.

1. Give each `Connection` a list attribute `_callback_problems`, empty when the connection is created. Every callback wrapper looks up the `Connection` for the `SSL` object it is called with (via `Connection._reverse_mapping`) before its `try` block, and on an exception appends it to that connection's `_callback_problems` and returns the same failure value as today.
2. Add `Connection._raise_callback_problem()`: if the connection has pending callback problems, clear OpenSSL's error queue (`ERR_clear_error`) and raise the oldest one (first in, first out). Call it at the start of `_raise_ssl_error` instead of asking the context's helpers, and in `DTLSv1_listen` instead of asking the cookie helpers.
3. Remove the `_CallbackExceptionHelper` base class; the helper classes no longer hold any exception state.
4. When creating the ALPN selection cffi callback, pass `error=SSL_TLSEXT_ERR_ALERT_FATAL`, so that if an exception ever escapes the wrapper OpenSSL gets a fatal alert instead of the default 0 (which would mean success).
5. Resulting behavior: an exception pending on one connection made from a context with an ALPN select callback does not affect a handshake on another connection made from the same context (which negotiates its protocol normally), and is still raised on its own connection at its next handshake attempt. A verify callback set with `Connection.set_verify` that raises makes the handshake fail with that very exception propagated to the caller.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.

accepted.subject: Recognize nested time zone names in TZ file paths (#186)
accepted.brief:
Make tzlocal recognise time zone names with more than one slash when the `TZ` environment variable points to a zone file.

Today `tzlocal.utils._tz_name_from_env` resolves a `TZ` value that is a file path (optionally prefixed with `:`) with `os.path.realpath` and only tries its last two path components (for example `Europe/Berlin`) and then its last component (for example `UTC`) as zone names.
